summary.text: At the prefix ending at 60, the restricted-growth value is the number of distinct preceding input values, and mapping each original input value to its associated triple is valid because every nonexceptional input has third coordinate 1. This map is not injective: the distinct exceptional inputs 56 and 60 both give \((A003415,A085731,A376418)=(92,4,2)\), so the triple prefix has strictly fewer distinct values and the two transforms differ at \(n=60\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=\operatorname{A003415}(n)
   =\sum_{p\mid n}v_p(n)\frac{n}{p},
\qquad
E(n)=\operatorname{A085731}(n)=\gcd(D(n),n),
\]
and let
\[
K(n)=\operatorname{A376418}(n)
   =\#\{k\geq 1:k^k\mid n\}.
\]
Also, let \(Q(n)=\operatorname{A359550}(n)\). Thus \(Q(n)=1\) precisely when no prime \(p\) satisfies \(p^p\mid n\), and \(Q(n)=0\) otherwise.

The function whose restricted growth transform is A379240 is
\[
f(n)=
\begin{cases}
P(D(n),E(n)),&Q(n)=1,\\
I(n),&Q(n)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Here \(P(a,b)\) denotes a value of “pair type” and \(I(n)\) a value of “integer type.” These two types are disjoint. This is merely a precise way to interpret the two different kinds of values in the definition: in particular, an integer-branch value can never equal a pair-branch value, \(I(m)=I(n)\) exactly when \(m=n\), and \(P(a,b)=P(c,d)\) exactly when \((a,b)=(c,d)\).

The function in the conjecture is the triple-valued function
\[
g(n)=(D(n),E(n),K(n)).
\]
We will prove that the restricted growth transforms of \(f\) and \(g\) differ at \(n=60\).

Recall explicitly what the restricted growth transform does. For a sequence \(h(1),h(2),\ldots\), list its distinct values in order of first occurrence and assign labels \(1,2,3,\ldots\) in that order. The restricted growth transform \(R_h(n)\) is the label of \(h(n)\). Equivalently, if \(h(n)\) is a new value, not occurring among \(h(1),\ldots,h(n-1)\), then
\[
R_h(n)=1+\#\{h(1),\ldots,h(n-1)\}.
\]
If \(h(n)=h(j)\), then \(R_h(n)=R_h(j)\).

We first establish the relation between \(f\) and \(g\).

**Lemma.** If \(Q(m)=1\), then \(K(m)=1\).

Indeed, \(1^1=1\) divides every positive integer \(m\), so \(k=1\) is always counted by \(K(m)\). Suppose, for contradiction, that some \(k\geq2\) also satisfies \(k^k\mid m\). Choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(k\). Then \(p\leq k\). Since \(p\mid k\), we have \(p^p\mid k^p\), and since \(p\leq k\), we have \(k^p\mid k^k\). Consequently
\[
p^p\mid k^k\mid m.
\]
But this contradicts \(Q(m)=1\), which says that no prime power \(p^p\) divides \(m\). Hence no \(k\geq2\) is counted, and the only counted value is \(k=1\). Therefore \(K(m)=1\).

Now define a map \(\rho\) from the possible values of \(f\) to triples by
\[
\rho(P(a,b))=(a,b,1),
\qquad
\rho(I(m))=(D(m),E(m),K(m)).
\]
We claim that
\[
g(m)=\rho(f(m))
\tag{1}
\]
for every positive integer \(m\). There are two cases.

* If \(Q(m)=1\), then \(f(m)=P(D(m),E(m))\). By the lemma, \(K(m)=1\), and hence
  \[
  \rho(f(m))=(D(m),E(m),1)=(D(m),E(m),K(m))=g(m).
  \]

* If \(Q(m)=0\), then \(f(m)=I(m)\), and the definition of \(\rho\) immediately gives
  \[
  \rho(f(m))=(D(m),E(m),K(m))=g(m).
  \]

Thus (1) holds in all cases. In particular, on every finite prefix the distinct \(g\)-values are the image under \(\rho\) of the distinct \(f\)-values. Therefore, for every \(N\),
\[
\#\{g(1),\ldots,g(N)\}
\leq
\#\{f(1),\ldots,f(N)\}.
\tag{2}
\]
The inequality can be strict because \(\rho\) need not be injective. The counterexample arises precisely from such a failure of injectivity.

We now compute the relevant data at \(56\) and \(60\).

First,
\[
56=2^3\cdot7.
\]
Thus
\[
D(56)
=3\frac{56}{2}+1\frac{56}{7}
=3\cdot28+8
=92.
\]
Similarly,
\[
60=2^2\cdot3\cdot5,
\]
so
\[
D(60)
=2\frac{60}{2}+\frac{60}{3}+\frac{60}{5}
=2\cdot30+20+12
=92.
\]
It follows that
\[
E(56)=\gcd(92,56)=4
\quad\text{and}\quad
E(60)=\gcd(92,60)=4.
\]
For example, \(92=4\cdot23\), \(56=4\cdot14\), and \(60=4\cdot15\), while neither gcd has any factor larger than \(4\).

Next we calculate \(K(56)\) and \(K(60)\). In both cases \(k=1\) is counted. Also \(k=2\) is counted because
\[
2^2=4\mid56
\quad\text{and}\quad
4\mid60.
\]
For \(k=3\), one has \(3^3=27\), which divides neither \(56\) nor \(60\). For every \(k\geq4\),
\[
k^k\geq4^4=256>60,
\]
so \(k^k\) cannot divide either positive integer \(56\) or \(60\). Hence exactly \(k=1,2\) are counted in each case, and
\[
K(56)=K(60)=2.
\]
Combining these calculations gives
\[
g(56)=(92,4,2)=g(60).
\tag{3}
\]

On the other hand, \(4=2^2\) divides both \(56\) and \(60\). Thus each is divisible by \(p^p\) for the prime \(p=2\), so
\[
Q(56)=Q(60)=0.
\]
They are therefore both in the integer branch of \(f\):
\[
f(56)=I(56),
\qquad
f(60)=I(60).
\tag{4}
\]
These values are distinct because \(56\ne60\). Nevertheless, by the definition of \(\rho\) and the computations above,
\[
\rho(I(56))=(92,4,2)=\rho(I(60)).
\]
Thus \(I(56)\) and \(I(60)\) are the two distinct original values that the triple construction identifies.

It remains to show carefully that this identification forces different restricted-growth labels at position \(60\), without needing to enumerate all earlier terms.

Let
\[
F_N=\{f(1),\ldots,f(N)\},
\qquad
G_N=\{g(1),\ldots,g(N)\}.
\]
Because of (1), \(G_N=\rho(F_N)\), and hence \(|G_N|\leq|F_N|\), as stated in (2).

The value \(f(60)=I(60)\) has not appeared at any earlier position. To see this, take \(j<60\). If \(Q(j)=1\), then \(f(j)\) is of pair type, so it cannot equal the integer-type value \(I(60)\). If \(Q(j)=0\), then \(f(j)=I(j)\), and \(I(j)\ne I(60)\) because \(j\ne60\). These two cases exhaust all \(j<60\). Therefore \(f(60)\) is new, and its restricted growth label is
\[
R_f(60)=|F_{59}|+1.
\tag{5}
\]

By contrast, equation (3) says that \(g(60)\) is not new: it is exactly the value already occurring at position \(56\). Hence
\[
R_g(60)=R_g(56).
\tag{6}
\]
The label of any value occurring by position \(56\) is at most the total number of distinct values occurring by that position. Thus
\[
R_g(56)\leq |G_{56}|.
\tag{7}
\]
Using the reduction \(g=\rho\circ f\), followed by inclusion of prefixes, gives
\[
|G_{56}|\leq |F_{56}|\leq |F_{59}|.
\tag{8}
\]
Combining (5)--(8), we obtain the strict inequality
\[
R_g(60)
=R_g(56)
\leq |G_{56}|
\leq |F_{56}|
\leq |F_{59}|
<|F_{59}|+1
=R_f(60).
\]
Therefore
\[
R_f(60)\ne R_g(60).
\]
But \(R_f\) is A379240, while \(R_g\) is the conjectured restricted growth transform of
\([\operatorname{A003415}(n),\operatorname{A085731}(n),\operatorname{A376418}(n)]\). Hence the two sequences already differ at \(n=60\), and the conjectured equality is false.
